extracted.intended_audience: federal judges, patent litigators, and counsel preparing jury instructions in U.S. patent litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions and accompanying practice guidance for use in U.S. patent litigation, including standards for claim construction, infringement, invalidity, damages, and related procedural points. Intended as templates to be tailored to the facts of a particular case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neutrality and tailoring of instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the fundamental goals of the Instructions is to provide a neutral set of jury instructions that would not be biased in favor of either the patent owner or the accused infringer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructions are not intended to address every conceivable issue; litigants must tailor these Instructions to the specific issues and facts in their case and eliminate superfluous or confusing instructions. Use bracketed terms and find-and-replace to insert case-specific facts. Practice Notes are for guidance and should not be included verbatim in jury instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent rights defined
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent gives the owner the right to exclude others from making, using, offering to sell, or selling the claimed invention within the United States or importing it into the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain to jurors that patents are granted by the USPTO and the application/specification/claims framework; claims define the scope of exclusive rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims define scope and are the only part infringed
rubrics_metrics.description: The purpose of the claims is to particularly point out what the applicant regards as the claimed invention and to define the scope of the patent owner’s exclusive rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only the claims of the patent can be infringed; written description and drawings are not themselves infringed. Use the same claim meaning for both infringement and invalidity determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability standards considered by examiner
rubrics_metrics.description: In examining a patent application, the Patent Examiner searches prior art and considers whether each claim defines an invention that is new, useful, and not obvious, whether the claims are directed to eligible subject matter, and whether the claims are definite, enabled, and adequately described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain prosecution history and Office Actions to jurors; prior art and patentability are described in jury instructions where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art—pre-AIA and AIA definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: [Prior Art (pre-AIA) — Knowledge that is available to the interested public either prior to the invention by the applicant or more than one year prior to the filing date of the application.] [Prior Art (AIA) — Knowledge that is publicly available before the effective filing date of the patent application.]
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice Note: Under AIA the Cutoff Date is the effective filing date; under pre-AIA the Cutoff Date can vary by claim and by §102 subsection. If different claims have different Cutoff Dates, jury instructions should address this and differences in the available prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof for infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: [The Plaintiff] must prove that [the Defendant] infringes one or more claims of the patent by a preponderance of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain preponderance of the evidence (more likely than not, i.e., slightly greater than 50%) and distinguish from criminal standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof for invalidity (clear and convincing)
rubrics_metrics.description: [The Defendant] must prove invalidity of each challenged claim by clear and convincing evidence in order to overcome the presumption of validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice Note: Consider substituting 'clear and convincing' with 'highly probable' or similar explanatory language to aid juror understanding. Explain that this standard sits between preponderance and beyond a reasonable doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge's role in claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the judge’s job to provide the meaning of any claim language that must be interpreted; the jury must accept and use the judge’s constructions for infringement and invalidity determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite governing case law (Phillips, Markman, Teva). Read stipulations and the court’s claim constructions to the jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function (§ 112 ¶ 6 / §112(f)) claim interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: When an element is expressed as a 'means' or 'step' for performing a function, the element is construed under §112: it covers the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents, not every means that performs the recited function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction 2.2 should be given only if the case involves means-plus-function claims. Provide the recited function and the corresponding structure from the specification; instruct jurors to use that interpretation for infringement and validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literal infringement requires every claim element
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent claim is literally infringed only if the accused product or method includes each and every element (or method step) in that patent claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurors must determine literal infringement with respect to each asserted claim; absence of even one element means no literal infringement of that claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of equivalents (DOE)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is infringed under the doctrine of equivalents only if there is an equivalent component/part/method step in the accused product/method for each claim element that is not literally present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff must prove equivalence by a preponderance of the evidence for each missing claim element. DOE is limited by prosecution history estoppel and subject matter dedicated to the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on DOE—prosecution history estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: Prosecution history estoppel can limit the application of the doctrine of equivalents where claim amendments or arguments in prosecution surrendered subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruct jurors about any relevant prosecution history estoppel and how it affects equivalence inquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on DOE—subject matter dedicated to the public
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine of equivalents does not cover subject matter that was dedicated to the public by the patent specification or prosecution history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruct jurors where portions of the specification or prosecution surrendered or dedicated subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct infringement—knowledge and intent immaterial
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge of the patent and intent to infringe are immaterial to a claim of direct infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain that direct infringement is a question of the accused product/method meeting the claim elements, regardless of the accused infringer’s awareness or intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint infringement / divided performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims may be directly infringed in circumstances involving multiple actors if one party exercises control or direction over the others or if the combined actions meet all claim limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide jury guidance on when joint or divided performance can give rise to direct infringement; adapt instructions to the evidence and contentions in the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement of means-plus-function or step-plus-function claims (literal and DOE)
rubrics_metrics.description: Literal infringement of means-plus-function claims requires that the accused device perform the claimed function using the structure in the specification (or equivalent). DOE analysis for such claims must consider the statutory and precedential constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give the special instruction for means-plus-function elements as required, and explain how equivalents are evaluated given the claim construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement of dependent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement of dependent claims is determined separately; dependent claims add additional limitations that must also be present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurors should evaluate each dependent claim individually for literal infringement or under DOE as applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction and meaning of transitional phrases ('comprising', 'consisting of', 'consisting essentially of')
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarify how transitional claim language affects claim scope (e.g., 'comprising' is inclusive; 'consisting of' is closed; 'consisting essentially of' permits unrecited elements that do not materially affect the basic and novel characteristics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide tailored instruction defining the transitional term(s) used in the asserted claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect infringement—inducement and contributory infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim may be indirectly infringed if a defendant induces another to infringe or contributes to another's infringement (e.g., by supplying a component especially made for use in the invention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish inducement from contributory infringement; instruct jurors on elements that must be proven for each form of indirect infringement under §271 and relevant case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement by supplying components abroad (§271(f)(1) & §271(f)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement can occur if a defendant supplies all or a substantial portion of the components of a patented invention for combination abroad (§271(f)(1)) or supplies components especially made/adapted for the invention into another country (§271(f)(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide instructions specific to the facts if supply-of-components theories are asserted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement by import/sale of product made by patented process (§271(g))
rubrics_metrics.description: A party may infringe if it imports, sells, offers to sell, or uses a product made by a patented process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide instruction on §271(g) when process claims and products made by patented processes are at issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary of invalidity defenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Defendant contends that asserted claims are invalid or unenforceable; the jury must decide invalidity for each challenged claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain that invalidity can be based on anticipation, obviousness, lack of written description, lack of enablement, or statutory bars, among others, and that defendant bears burden by clear and convincing evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA)
rubrics_metrics.description: [Ordinary skill in the art (pre-AIA) — The level of experience, education, or training generally possessed by those individuals who work in the area of the invention at the time of the invention.] [Ordinary skill in the art (AIA) — The level of experience, education, or training generally possessed by those individuals who work in the area of the invention before the effective filing date of the patent.]
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurors should use the defined POSITA when assessing obviousness, enablement, written description, and other invalidity questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation—prior public knowledge and printed publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipation requires that the claimed invention was known or described in the prior art (including prior public knowledge and printed publications) before the Cutoff Date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate AIA and pre-AIA Cutoff Date rules; evaluate whether a reference qualifies as prior art and whether it discloses every element of the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior public use and on-sale bar (pre-AIA and AIA distinctions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior public use and the on-sale bar can invalidate claims if the invention was publicly used or on sale prior to the Cutoff Date; AIA and pre-AIA law treat timing and particulars differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give separate instructions for pre-AIA and AIA scenarios as set out in the model instructions; consider experimental use exceptions where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Earlier-filed patent application and prior patent references
rubrics_metrics.description: Earlier-filed patent applications and prior patents may constitute prior art depending on AIA vs pre-AIA rules and can affect anticipation and obviousness analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide the appropriate pre-AIA/AIA instructions on earlier-filed patent documents and their weight as prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness—Graham factors / four-factor framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness should be assessed using (1) the scope and content of the prior art, (2) differences between the claimed invention and the prior art, (3) the level of ordinary skill in the art, and (4) secondary considerations (other considerations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain how to apply these factors and weigh them collectively; include examples of secondary considerations such as commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, and failure of others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement requirement (§112)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must teach those skilled in the art how to make and use the claimed invention so as to enable them to do so without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruct jurors on the enablement inquiry and relevant evidence bearing on whether the specification enables the full scope of claimed embodiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written-description requirement (§112)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must adequately describe the invention and show that the inventor was in possession of the claimed invention at the time of filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurors should evaluate written-description evidence separately from enablement evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages—general principles
rubrics_metrics.description: If infringement is proven, the patent owner may recover damages to compensate for harm, including lost profits, price erosion, cost escalation, convoyed sales, or a reasonable royalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain that damages are compensatory (not punitive) and that the plaintiff bears the burden to prove the amount of damages by a preponderance of the evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost profits standard and types of damages
rubrics_metrics.description: Lost profits are recoverable when the patent owner shows but-for causation (the patentee would have made the sales but for the infringement). Other recoverable items include price erosion, cost escalation, and convoyed sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply appropriate economic evidence and legal tests (e.g., Panduit or other applicable tests as relevant to the jurisdiction and case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty—hypothetical negotiation framework
rubrics_metrics.description: A reasonable royalty is determined by what a hypothetical negotiation between the patent owner and accused infringer would have produced at the time the infringement began.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of foreseeability, post-infringement licenses, profits, non-infringing alternatives, and other factors may be considered. Avoid hindsight and account for what parties would have reasonably anticipated at the negotiation date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entire market value rule (EMVR) and apportionment
rubrics_metrics.description: Awards based on a percentage of revenues of an entire multi-component product are generally inappropriate unless the patented feature is the sole driver of customer demand or substantially creates the value of the product (the EMVR narrow exception).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require patentee to show that the patented feature is the basis for customer demand; otherwise instruct jurors to apportion damages to the value attributable to the patented feature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty—multiple patents
rubrics_metrics.description: If multiple patents are infringed, the jury may award separate royalties for each patent and consider the number of licenses needed for the product when assessing the hypothetical negotiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for the aggregate effect of multiple licenses on the hypothetical negotiation and apportionment across patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty—timing and foreseeability
rubrics_metrics.description: Damages should reflect the hypothetical negotiation at the time it would have occurred; evidence of events after that date may be considered only to the extent they were reasonably foreseeable at the negotiation date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurors may consider later licenses and uses where appropriate to the foreseeability inquiry, but should not base damages on pure hindsight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty—availability of non-infringing substitutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider evidence on the availability and cost of acceptable non-infringing substitutes when determining a reasonable royalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An acceptable substitute must either be licensed under the patent or not infringe; substitute availability can reduce a reasonable royalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty—use of comparable license agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: Jurors may consider prior license agreements and comparable transactions when determining a reasonable royalty, but must account for differences between those licenses and the hypothetical license in question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust for technological, economic, and party differences between comparable licenses and the hypothetical negotiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doubts on damages resolved against infringer for poor recordkeeping
rubrics_metrics.description: Any doubts about damages resulting from the defendant’s failure to keep proper records should be resolved in favor of the plaintiff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confusion or lack of records caused by the defendant should be held against the defendant when assessing damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard-Essential Patents (SEPs) and FRAND
rubrics_metrics.description: For SEPs, instruct the jury on the particulars of any FRAND/SSO commitment, apply established patent law principles, and include only Georgia-Pacific factors relevant to the case; instruct on apportionment both to the portion of the standard and to the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not instruct the jury on irrelevant Georgia-Pacific factors; carefully frame apportionment and FRAND commitments as they relate to the asserted SEP(s).

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful infringement—standard
rubrics_metrics.description: If infringement is found, the jury must determine whether the infringement was willful. Plaintiff must prove by a preponderance of the evidence that the defendant knew of the patent and intentionally infringed at least one asserted claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the defendant’s behavior was deliberate or intentional and assess all circumstances and the defendant’s knowledge at the time of the conduct. A mere knowledge of the patent, without deliberate or intentional infringement, is insufficient to prove willfulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful infringement—reliance on legal opinion and §298
rubrics_metrics.description: The failure to obtain an opinion of counsel may not be used to prove willfulness (§298). If the defendant relies on a legal opinion, the jury may consider reasonable reliance on a competent opinion as a factor in the totality of circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modify instruction depending on whether the defendant asserts reliance on counsel; do not allow absence of a legal opinion alone to support willfulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Practice Notes and bracketed terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice Notes are provided as practical guidance but are not statements of law and are not intended to be included in jury instructions. Bracketed terms (e.g., [the Plaintiff], [claims in dispute]) are provided for find-and-replace customization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Customize bracketed language to case facts; remove instructions or alternatives not applicable to the case (e.g., if doctrine of equivalents or certain defenses are not at issue).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial procedure basics for jurors (evidence vs argument)
rubrics_metrics.description: Opening statements and closing arguments are not evidence; jurors must decide based only on evidence admitted during trial. Depositions may be used as evidence and are to be considered as if the witness testified live.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruct jurors to keep an open mind and wait until all evidence is presented before making decisions; explain the phases of a jury trial and deliberation procedures.
